fact: CSU Extension's PlantTalk Colorado says female cottonwoods shed their cotton in June, often so heavily that nearby lawns turn white, and that the cotton carries the trees' small seeds on the wind.
quote: Cotton shed by female trees in June is often so abundant that it turns nearby lawns white. … Flowers on female trees, after being pollinated by wind-borne pollen from male trees in April, develop small green capsules that split open in June to shed small seeds carried by wind-borne “cotton”.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1758: Cottonwood Cotton

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says even tiny debris such as seeds or small twigs can affect a putt on a home putting green, and advises a leaf blower on a low setting daily or before each use.
quote: Even tiny debris like seeds or small twigs can affect a putt. Use a leaf blower on a low setting daily or before each use to keep the surface immaculate.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (home putting green section)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says the amount and condition of a home putting green's infill directly affect how the ball rolls, so the green needs regular brushing to keep the infill even and may need topping off to hold its speed.
quote: The amount and condition of the infill directly impact how the ball rolls. Your installer can provide specific guidance, but generally, you’ll need to brush the green regularly to keep the infill evenly distributed and may need to top it off to maintain the desired speed.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (home putting green section)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says a home putting green may need rolling with a water-filled lawn roller now and then to keep it smooth and fast, because rolling compacts the infill for a consistent ball speed.
quote: To keep the surface perfectly smooth and fast, you may need to roll it with a water-filled lawn roller periodically. This helps compact the infill for a consistent ball speed.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (home putting green section)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape advises keeping dirty shoes off a home putting green and keeping a pair of soft-soled shoes just for the green, so dirt and debris are not tracked onto it.
quote: Avoid walking on your putting green with dirty shoes. Keep a dedicated pair of soft-soled shoes for use on the green to prevent tracking dirt and debris onto the pristine surface.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (home putting green section)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says infill gets displaced from high-traffic areas or washes out in heavy rain, that you can check it by parting the fibers with your fingers to see it covering the backing, and that a top-up should use the same infill as the original, spread thin with a drop spreader and broomed down into the fibers.
quote: Over time, infill can get displaced from high-traffic areas or wash out from heavy rains. You can check the levels by parting the grass fibers with your fingers. You should see the infill clearly covering the backing. … Purchase the same type of infill that was originally installed. Use a drop spreader to apply a thin layer over the area, then use your broom to work it down into the base of the fibers.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (home putting green section)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape warns that a leaf blower's high air pressure can displace or remove infill, and advises a low-power setting, a safe distance from the turf and gentle sweeping motions.
quote: However, it should be used with caution, as high air pressure can displace or remove the infill. Opt for a low-power setting, keep the blower at a safe distance from the turf, and use gentle sweeping motions to avoid disturbing the infill.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (home putting green section)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape advises a thorough spring cleaning after winter's debris, by raking, brushing and rinsing, and says fall leaves left over winter can decompose into a layer that impedes drainage and encourages moss.
quote: Spring: After winter, your lawn may have accumulated a lot of debris. Perform a thorough cleaning by raking, brushing, and rinsing the entire surface. … Autumn: As leaves begin to fall, it’s important to remove them regularly. If left to sit over winter, they can decompose and create a layer of organic matter that can impede drainage and encourage moss growth.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (home putting green section)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says to let snow on turf melt and drain away, to clear a path only with a plastic shovel or, for light powdery snow, a leaf blower, and never to use a metal shovel, which can tear turf, or rock salt.
quote: let snow melt naturally and drain away. If you must clear a path, use a plastic shovel or a leaf blower for light, powdery snow. Never use a metal shovel, which can tear the turf, or rock salt, which can clog the drainage system and damage the backing.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (home putting green section)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says many professional turf installers offer an annual maintenance service that deep cleans the surface, checks the seams and tops up the infill.
quote: many professional turf installers offer an annual maintenance service. They will use specialized sports turf maintenance equipment to deep clean the surface, check seam integrity, and top up the turf infill levels for you.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (home putting green section)

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's 2013 field maintenance guidelines say infill settles into new synthetic turf over several months of use and rainfall, that more frequent brushing may be advised during that period, and that infill depth should be checked for consistency once it has settled.
quote: After a period of several months of initial use of the field and rainfall, the infill material will settle into the synthetic turf. During this period, more frequent brushing may be advised by your field builder. Once settling occurs, check the infill depth for consistency around the field and to ensure it is within the field builder’s guidelines.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)
notes: Written for infilled sports fields, not backyard greens; the page says so.

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's field guidelines advise checking infill levels after heavy rainfall, in case infill has migrated with the slope.
quote: After heavy rainfall, it is advisable to check the infill levels in case of migration with the field slope.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's field guidelines say that to keep infill from moving when blowing debris off, the nozzle should not point directly into the turf and the blower should run at minimal throttle.
quote: To minimize or eliminate the movement of infill, do not point nozzle directly into the turf. Use minimal throttle to decrease the volume of air.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's field guidelines say leaves and other airborne debris left on the surface migrate into the turf, where they inhibit drainage and compact the infill.
quote: Remove airborne contaminants, such as leaves and other debris. If allowed to remain on the surface for any length of time, they will migrate into the system, inhibiting drainage and causing infill compaction.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's field guidelines name an infill depth gauge, or a nail and tape measure used on a grid, as the preferred way to measure infill depth and consistency.
quote: Using an infill depth gauge or a nail and tape measure on a grid pattern is the preferred way to measure infill depth and consistency.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist says seasonal maintenance is crucial for a synthetic putting green: foot traffic makes dips where the same putts are hit again and again, the areas around the cups get uneven and slow, and the fix is to inspect the infill depth and roll the whole surface.
quote: Seasonal maintenance is crucial for a synthetic turf putting green. … Continuous foot traffic alone can cause dips and valleys where repetitive putts are made. Fibers flip up due to friction and dragging of the feet or shoes. Areas around the cups start to become uneven and slow. When issues like these arise, you will need to inspect the infill depths and roll the entire surface.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Rolling Putting Green Surfaces

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist says a putting green can be rolled with a sod water roller bought from a landscape supply or rented, that rolling in freezing temperatures takes longer because cold fibers are slow to press down to the infill, that the roller should cross the green in many directions (12 to 6, 3 to 9, 2 to 8, 10 to 4), and that the fringe and the lawn turf around the green should not be rolled.
quote: You can purchase a sod water roller from your nearest landscape supply house, or many rental places have them for rent. … Temperature can make or break a good rolling. If you are trying to roll a putting green in freezing temperatures, it will take longer for the fibers to depress to the infill. … Go 12 to 6, 3 to 9, 2 to 8, 10 to 4, etc. … DO NOT ROLL EXTERIOR FRINGE OR CONNECTING LANDSCAPE TURF, FOR THIS MAY DAMAGE THE FIBERS AND/OR CAUSE MATTING
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Rolling Putting Green Surfaces

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist recommends inspecting a putting green every season, so the infill depth stays at the manufacturer's specification, repairs get made and the surface is kept free of debris.
quote: I recommend inspecting the installation every season to ensure that the infill depths are at the manufacturer’s specifications, repairs are made, and the surface is kept clean of any debris
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Perfecting Putting Green Surfaces, Part 2: Infill Placement

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist says sand put into putting green turf that holds any moisture sticks to the fibers instead of dropping to the base, and hurts how the ball rolls and the green's speed.
quote: If you are intending to place infill into putting green materials that have any moisture within them, it will have an adverse effect on the way the ball rolls and Stimpmeter speeds. … When moisture meets synthetic turf fibers, it sticks to the fibers and prevents infill from dropping into the base of the synthetic turf.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Perfecting Putting Green Surfaces, Part 2: Infill Placement

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist says not to drop too much sand into a putting green at one time, to cross the drop-spreader passes east to west and then north to south, and to avoid beach sand, coal slag, dirty silica and fine cement sand.
quote: When dropping infill sand into your putting green, it is very important NOT to place too much at one time. … I recommend making passes with the drop spreader starting from east to west and then north to south. … Avoid using materials like beach sand, coal slag, dirty silica, or fine cement sand.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Perfecting Putting Green Surfaces, Part 2: Infill Placement

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist says synthetic turf expands as it warms and contracts as it cools, that sun and heat can wrinkle turf and putting greens especially, and that infill ballast is what controls the movement.
quote: Like concrete, synthetic turf expands as the temperature rises and contracts as the temperature falls. … UV sunlight gives off thermal radiation generated by the hot plasma of the sun and will cause synthetic turf to wrinkle, especially putting greens. … Ballas is the most effective way to control thermal contraction and expansion in putting greens.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Perfecting Putting Green Surfaces, Part 2: Infill Placement
notes: The source spells ballast as 'Ballas' in that sentence; quoted as printed.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist says the amount of infill sets a putting green's speed: more infill firms the surface and speeds the roll, while too little lets it wrinkle and slows it down.
quote: The amount and type of infill you use directly affects the green speed. … More infill firms up the surface and increases roll speed. Less infill causes wrinkles and slows it down.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, How to Make Your Backyard Putting Green PGA-Level Quality

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist says cups set in compacted dirt tend to shift as rainwater, foot traffic and pulling the flag loosen the soil, recommends setting cups in concrete, performance concrete where frost heave is high, and says an unstable cup can settle or push up the surface around it.
quote: I highly recommend placing putting green cups in concrete. And for areas that have high frost-heave, please use performance concrete. When placing putting green cups in compacted dirt, the cups tend to shift due to loosening soil caused by rainwater, foot traffic, and excessively pulling the flag in and out of the cup. When the putting green cup is unstable, it can cause the cup to move or settle, which can tilt the flags and/or trigger the “volcano effect”.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, How to Make Your Backyard Putting Green PGA-Level Quality

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist says runoff from outside a putting green often seeps in under the surface and leads to settling and depressions, and lists settlement and frost heave among the causes of putting green surface failures.
quote: Exterior runoff and areas outside the putting green often seep in and below the surface, leading to settling and depressions. … Contractors, installers, and even homeowners must all learn what causes putting green surfaces to fail. This includes unevenness, dips, bumps, ridges, lines, protrusions, expansion, contraction, seam rupture, settlement, frost-heave, rough, pitted, you name it, the uncertain.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, How to Make Your Backyard Putting Green PGA-Level Quality

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer columnist says most putting green turf is made without drainage holes in the backing, so on a green built flat and level, storm water has nowhere to go and can be trapped by the fringe during a heavy storm.
quote: most putting green materials are manufactured without drainage holes punched into the backing. … Now, if your green is completely flat and level, water has nowhere to go. It can get trapped by the exterior fringe, and during a heavy storm, that trapped water can cause serious issues.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Why Don't Putting Greens Have Drainage Holes?

fact: In a 1990 USGA Green Section Record article, turfgrass researcher A. Douglas Brede reported that most of the students he tested could not tell a 2.2% slope from level, advised not relying on your eyes to judge whether a spot is level, and said to avoid concave or convex spots when measuring green speed.
quote: Most were unable to distinguish a 2.2% slope from level. Thus, don't rely on your sight to tell you if you're on a level area. … Try to avoid areas with concave or convex surfaces, just as you would when reading traditional stimpmeter speed.
source_label: A. Douglas Brede, Measuring Green Speed on Sloped Putting Greens, USGA Green Section Record, November/December 1990
notes: Read from the scanned magazine article in Michigan State University's Turfgrass Information Center archive of the Green Section Record.

fact: The Motz Group, an infill maker, says to pick up sticks and debris a few times a year, particularly after a storm or heavy winds, that a leaf blower held about 12 to 18 inches above the turf should not move the infill, and that a blower may not suit wet leaves clumped together after heavy rain.
quote: Before you start raking leaves, walk around your lawn and pick up all the larger sticks or debris. It’s good to do this a few times per year, particularly when there’s been a storm or heavy winds. … Leaf blowers make a quick task of dried leaves and debris, but they may not be your best option after a big storm or heavy rain when leaves are clumped together and heavier. As long as you keep the leaf blower at a distance of about 12-18 inches above your artificial turf, you should avoid any potential infill migration.
source_label: The Motz Group, How to Rake Leaves on Artificial Turf Without Causing Damage

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's field guidelines suggest covering a field with an approved tarp when it is not in use to keep leaves and debris off, but warn against a tarp in freezing weather, since one that is not vinyl- or poly-coated can freeze to the surface and be very hard to remove.
quote: Remove airborne contaminants, such as leaves and other debris. If allowed to remain on the surface for any length of time, they will migrate into the system, inhibiting drainage and causing infill compaction. Consider covering the field with pre-approved tarp when it is not in use. … Avoid using a tarp on the field during freezing weather. Tarps, unless vinyl or poly-coated, can freeze to the surface, and will be very difficult to remove.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says a pressure washer can be used on artificial turf only with great caution: a wide-angle nozzle, at least a foot from the surface and under 1,500 PSI, to avoid damaging the fibers and blasting out the infill.
quote: Yes, but with great caution. Use a wide-angle nozzle, keep it at least one foot away from the surface, and ensure the pressure is low (under 1500 PSI). This prevents damage to the fibers and avoids blasting out the crucial turf infill.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (home putting green section)
